patient.name: Terry Walsh
patient.setting: GP surgery, then respiratory clinic and pleural unit
patient.complaint: Two years of slowly worsening breathlessness, now with right-sided chest pain
background: Pipe lagger in the Woolwich docks and shipyards, 1968–1990
Smoker, 35 pack-years, still smoking 10 a day
Lives with his wife in Eltham

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an occupational clue (builder, shipyard, insulation) decades before: progressive breathlessness, clubbing and basal crackles mean asbestosis; chest pain, weight loss and an effusion mean mesothelioma; isolated calcified plaques are benign.

points: Terry, 72, breathless walking up his road for 2 years.
Worked **lagging pipes with asbestos** in the shipyards for 22 years.

steps.lead: Terry's job decades ago is the key: asbestos causes **fibrosis, pleural disease and cancer**, after a very long latency.
Terry has **asbestosis**: progressive breathlessness, cough, bibasal crackles and reduced expansion, with **lower lobe** fibrosis and plaques on the X-ray.

steps.title: The asbestos spectrum
head: Disease
Symptoms
Key finding
Malignant?
rows: Calcified plaques on diaphragm and lower lateral chest wall

steps.lead: Terry's CXR also shows calcified **pleural plaques**: a marker of exposure 20 to 40 years ago, harmless on their own.

points: Eighteen months later: dull ache in the **right chest wall**.
More breathless; one streak of blood in his sputum.
Right base **stony dull** with absent breath sounds.

steps.q: Terry now has chest wall pain, weight loss and a right effusion. What do you fear most?
steps.r: Chest pain, weight loss and a unilateral effusion in an asbestos worker is **mesothelioma** until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Terry's story fits **mesothelioma**: decades of latency, then chest pain, weight loss, haemoptysis and a stony dull effusion.
As a **smoker** with asbestos exposure, Terry also has a hugely raised lung cancer risk, and mesothelioma often first shows as an effusion.

visual.caption: Exposure ended in 1990; plaques, asbestosis and mesothelioma appear decades later.

steps.text: Pleural plaques do **not** turn into mesothelioma and need no follow-up. Do not pick 'surveillance CT' for isolated plaques.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (chest X-ray), 'confirm the diagnosis' (CT with occupational history), and 'confirm mesothelioma' (thoracoscopy and pleural biopsy), plus spirometry showing a restrictive pattern.

steps.q: Which test does the GP request first for Terry?
steps.r: A **chest X-ray** is first-line: plaques, fibrosis, effusion or thickening.

steps.lead: Terry's first **CXR** shows lower zone reticular shadowing and calcified plaques along both hemidiaphragms.

visual.title: Terry's first chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral lower zone fibrosis, with calcified plaques along the diaphragms.

steps.title: Lung function
steps.text: Both volumes down with a preserved ratio: restrictive. Low gas transfer from fibrosis.

visual.title: FEV1/FVC ratio
visual.label: Terry 0.86
visual.caption: A ratio above 0.7 with a low FVC is a restrictive pattern.

steps.lead: Terry's **CT chest** plus his detailed **occupational history** confirm asbestosis with pleural plaques.

visual.title: Terry's chest X-ray 18 months later
visual.caption: New large right pleural effusion on a background of basal fibrosis.

steps.title: Pleural fluid (ultrasound-guided aspiration)
steps.text: Exudate. Cytology is often non-diagnostic in mesothelioma.

steps.lead: Terry's CT shows nodular right pleural thickening; **thoracoscopy and pleural biopsy** confirm epithelioid **mesothelioma** on histology.

steps.text: Pleural fluid cytology is often **negative** in mesothelioma. A tissue diagnosis needs **thoracoscopic pleural biopsy**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (smoking cessation and avoiding further exposure), 'reassurance only' for pleural plaques, and draining a symptomatic effusion in mesothelioma.

steps.q: Terry has asbestosis and still smokes. What is the single most important step?
steps.r: **Smoking cessation**: smoking and asbestos multiply his lung cancer risk.

steps.lead: Terry is referred to the stop smoking service with varenicline, and told to avoid any further asbestos exposure. His plaques alone need only reassurance.

visual.title: Relative lung cancer risk
visual.label: Terry about 50x
visual.caption: The risks multiply rather than add: stopping smoking is the biggest win.

steps.lead: Terry joins **pulmonary rehabilitation**, and his lung function and imaging are monitored in clinic; oxygen is assessed if he becomes hypoxic.

steps.title: Managing Terry's mesothelioma
nodes: Drain it (therapeutic aspiration or chest drain)
Recurs: indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis
MDT: treat per type and stage

steps.lead: Terry's effusion is **drained** and his mesothelioma is treated according to its type and stage by the lung cancer MDT.
Terry's plaques needed **no follow-up**, and the **20 to 40 year latency** explains why his disease appeared long after he left the docks.

steps.text: Asbestosis and mesothelioma are **prescribed industrial diseases**: patients can claim compensation, and deaths are reported to the coroner.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: how asbestos causes fibrosis (macrophages, reactive oxygen species), why amphibole fibres cause mesothelioma, and why smoking multiplies risk.

steps.lead: Fibres reach Terry's **distal airways**; macrophages cannot clear them and keep releasing inflammatory mediators and **reactive oxygen species**.

steps.title: Fibre to fibrosis
nodes: Macrophages try and fail to engulf them

steps.q: Why is Terry's fibrosis worst at the bases?
o: Gravity drags fibres into the pleura
Upper lobes are protected by mucus
steps.r: The **lower lobes** get more ventilation, so more inhaled fibres are deposited there.

steps.lead: Fibres that migrated to Terry's pleura caused **localised calcified plaques**: a scar of exposure, not a step towards cancer.
Terry's mesothelioma came from **amphibole fibres** (blue and brown asbestos) damaging mesothelial cell DNA over decades.
Terry's cigarettes and his asbestos work **synergistically**, so his lung cancer risk is multiplied, not just added.

steps.text: Smoking does **not** raise mesothelioma risk; it multiplies **lung cancer** risk in asbestos-exposed people.

mcq.q: What is the most important risk factor for asbestos-related lung disease?
Which lung zones are mainly affected in asbestosis?
mcq.r: Asbestosis is **lower lobe** predominant (unlike silicosis and coal pneumoconiosis).

mcq.q: Are pleural plaques associated with an increased cancer risk?
mcq.r: Plaques are **benign**, with no malignant change and no follow-up needed.

mcq.q: How long after exposure do pleural plaques typically appear?
mcq.r: They indicate exposure **20 to 40 years** earlier.

mcq.q: Which examination finding suggests a pleural effusion in mesothelioma?
mcq.r: **Stony dull** percussion with reduced breath sounds.

mcq.q: What is the first-line investigation for suspected asbestos-related lung disease?
mcq.r: A **chest X-ray** shows plaques, fibrosis or effusion.

mcq.q: What confirms a diagnosis of mesothelioma?
Which lung function pattern does asbestosis give?
mcq.r: A **restrictive** pattern: low FEV1 and FVC with a preserved ratio.

mcq.q: What is the most important lifestyle step in asbestos-related lung disease?
mcq.r: **Smoking cessation** with support, given the synergistic lung cancer risk.

mcq.q: Which fibre type is most carcinogenic to mesothelial cells?
mcq.r: **Amphibole** fibres (crocidolite, amosite) are directly genotoxic to mesothelial cells.

prompts.q: What is asbestos-related lung disease and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look for the job in the stem, often decades before.

points.why: Know all four: plaques, asbestosis, mesothelioma, lung cancer.
Disease appears 20 to 40 years after exposure.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: builder + clubbing + basal crackles = asbestosis.

points.why: Common in asbestosis; not caused by plaques.

points.p: Lower lobe predominant fibrosis with pleural plaques on CXR
points.why: Silicosis and coal pneumoconiosis are upper zone.

prompts.q: What is the classic presentation of mesothelioma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: asbestos worker with chest pain, weight loss and a unilateral effusion.

points.why: With reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance.

points.p: Very long latent period after exposure

prompts.q: What are pleural plaques and what do they mean for the patient?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the answer is reassurance.

points.p: On the lower lateral chest wall and diaphragm, often calcified
Marker of exposure 20 to 40 years earlier
points.why: Not a disease process in themselves.

points.p: Benign: no malignant change, no increased cancer risk, no follow-up

prompts.q: Which complications does asbestos exposure lead to, and how does smoking change risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: smoking multiplies lung cancer, not mesothelioma.

points.p: Lung cancer risk markedly increased with asbestos plus smoking
Mesothelioma, which can present with an effusion

prompts.q: What are the first-line and confirmatory investigations?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: CXR first; CT plus the occupational history confirms.

points.p: Chest X-ray first-line: plaques, fibrosis, effusion or thickening
points.why: Unilateral effusion raises concern for mesothelioma.

points.p: CT chest (more sensitive) for plaques, fibrosis, malignancy

points.why: CT plus history is the gold standard.
Low FEV1 and FVC, ratio above 0.7, low TLCO.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tissue is the issue.

points.why: Direct view of the pleura with biopsy.
Pleural fluid cytology is often non-diagnostic.

prompts.q: How is asbestos-related lung disease managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stop smoking first; plaques need nothing; effusions get drained.

points.why: The most important step: synergistic cancer risk.

points.p: Supportive: oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, monitor lung function and imaging
Severe: drain effusions; treat malignancy by type and stage
points.why: Recurrent effusions may need an indwelling catheter or pleurodesis.

prompts.q: How does asbestos cause fibrosis, plaques and mesothelioma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: macrophages for fibrosis, amphiboles for mesothelioma.

points.p: Fibres deposit in distal airways and pleura
Macrophages release inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen species
Plaques: fibres irritate the pleura, causing localised calcified plaques
Amphibole fibres are directly genotoxic to mesothelial cells

glossary.Asbestos: A naturally occurring fibrous mineral once widely used for insulation, lagging and building materials.
glossary.Asbestosis: Interstitial lung fibrosis caused by inhaled asbestos fibres.
glossary.Mesothelioma: A malignant tumour of the pleura (or peritoneum), strongly linked to asbestos.
glossary.Mesothelial cells: The cells lining the pleura and peritoneum, from which mesothelioma arises.
glossary.Pleural plaques: Benign, often calcified patches of pleural thickening that mark past asbestos exposure.
glossary.Pleura: The thin membranes lining the lungs and inner chest wall.
glossary.Pleural effusion: Fluid collecting between the two layers of the pleura.
glossary.Pleural thickening: Fibrous thickening of the pleura; diffuse or nodular thickening may suggest mesothelioma.
glossary.Latency: The time between exposure and disease appearing; decades for asbestos.
glossary.Amphibole: The straight, needle-like asbestos fibre group (crocidolite, amosite) most linked to mesothelioma.
glossary.Crocidolite: Blue asbestos, an amphibole and the most carcinogenic type.
glossary.Chrysotile: White, curly serpentine asbestos; less carcinogenic than amphiboles.
glossary.Lagger: A worker who wraps pipes and boilers with insulation, historically asbestos.
glossary.Clubbing: Loss of the nail-bed angle and bulbous fingertips, seen in asbestosis and lung cancer.
glossary.Bibasal crackles: Crackles heard at both lung bases; fine and end-inspiratory in fibrosis.
glossary.Stony dull: A very dull percussion note over fluid, classic of a pleural effusion.
glossary.Restrictive pattern: Low FEV1 and FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio, as in fibrosis.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity: total air blown out after a full breath in.
glossary.TLCO: Transfer factor for carbon monoxide: how well gas crosses into the blood; low in fibrosis.
glossary.HRCT: High-resolution CT, used to show lung fibrosis and pleural disease in detail.
glossary.Thoracoscopy: A camera passed into the pleural space to inspect and biopsy the pleura.
glossary.Cytology: Looking at cells under the microscope; often non-diagnostic for mesothelioma in pleural fluid.
glossary.Histology: Examining tissue under the microscope to make a definitive diagnosis.
glossary.Exudate: Protein-rich pleural fluid from inflammation or malignancy (protein above 30 g/L or by Light's criteria).
glossary.Reactive oxygen species: Damaging oxygen-containing molecules released by macrophages that injure tissue and DNA.
glossary.Macrophages: Immune cells that engulf particles; they fail to clear asbestos fibres and drive inflammation.
glossary.Genotoxic: Damaging to DNA, causing mutations that can lead to cancer.
glossary.Synergistic: Two factors combining to give an effect greater than their sum.
glossary.Pulmonary rehabilitation: A supervised exercise and education programme that improves breathlessness and exercise tolerance.
glossary.Pleurodesis: Sealing the pleural space (e.g. with talc) to stop an effusion recurring.
glossary.Indwelling pleural catheter: A tunnelled tube left in the chest so a recurrent effusion can be drained at home.
glossary.Silicosis: Fibrosis from silica dust, mainly upper zone, with eggshell calcification of hilar nodes.
glossary.MDT: Multidisciplinary team meeting that plans cancer treatment.
glossary.Varenicline: A partial nicotinic agonist used to help people stop smoking.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has a 3 month history of a dull ache in his left chest and 6 kg weight loss. He worked as a boiler engineer for 30 years and has never smoked. There is stony dull percussion with absent breath sounds at the left base. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis in someone with an occupational clue.

clues: dull ache in his left chest
steps.x: Asbestos exposure, chest pain, weight loss and a unilateral effusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Malignant mesothelioma**.

elim: Asbestosis is fibrosis: crackles and breathlessness, not pain and an effusion.
Empyema would cause fever and sepsis.
Heart failure gives bilateral effusions and no weight loss or chest pain.
TB gives fever and night sweats; the occupational clue points to asbestos.

steps.x: **D. Mesothelioma.** Asbestos job + chest pain + weight loss + effusion.

technique.stem: A 69 year old retired electrician has a 1 year history of gradually worsening breathlessness. He handled asbestos insulation boards in the 1970s. There are fine crackles at both lung bases and his fingers are clubbed. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation: the first test, not the best.

clues: fine crackles at both lung bases
steps.x: Suspected asbestosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest X-ray** first.

elim: Bronchoscopy is for central masses or haemoptysis.
HRCT is more sensitive but comes after the CXR.
Pleural biopsy is for suspected mesothelioma.
Spirometry shows restriction but does not diagnose the cause.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** Then CT and an occupational history to confirm.

technique.stem: A 71 year old former shipyard worker has asbestosis confirmed on CT. He stopped smoking 10 years ago. He is breathless walking 200 metres. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. His FVC is 64% predicted.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Pulmonary rehabilitation with lung function monitoring

steps.x: Long-term management of asbestosis.
Already an ex-smoker, so the next step is supportive care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Supportive care**: pulmonary rehab, monitor lung function and imaging, oxygen if needed.

elim: Bronchoscopy has no role in monitoring asbestosis.
Steroids do not help asbestosis.
Methotrexate is not used for asbestosis.
Azithromycin prophylaxis is for bronchiectasis or COPD exacerbations.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary rehabilitation with monitoring.** No drug reverses asbestosis.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man who worked spraying blue asbestos (crocidolite) in the 1970s is diagnosed with pleural mesothelioma. He has never smoked. His brother, who worked with him, has only pleural plaques.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his tumour?
o: Amphibole fibre genotoxicity in mesothelial cells

steps.x: A mechanism of carcinogenesis.
Crocidolite is an amphibole; no smoking.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Amphibole fibres** directly damage mesothelial cell DNA over decades.

elim: EBV is linked to lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer.
BRCA2 is linked to breast, ovarian and prostate cancer.
Radon is linked to lung cancer, not mesothelioma.
He never smoked, and smoking does not cause mesothelioma.

steps.x: **A. Amphibole genotoxicity.** Plaques in his brother are just a marker of exposure.

practice.stem: A 75 year old man has 3 years of slowly worsening breathlessness and a dry cough. He worked in a shipyard fitting insulation for 25 years. His fingers are clubbed and there are fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. HRCT shows bilateral lower zone fibrosis with calcified pleural plaques.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Lower zone fibrosis with pleural plaques, clubbing and crackles in a shipyard insulation worker is asbestosis. Silicosis affects the upper zones.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a fibrotic lung disease.

clues: fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
lower zone fibrosis with calcified pleural plaques
steps.x: Asbestos exposure, basal fibrosis and plaques.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Asbestosis**.

elim: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis needs an antigen (birds, mould) and is upper or mid zone.
Lymphangitis is spread of cancer, with weight loss.
Sarcoidosis gives bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in younger people.
Silicosis is upper zone with hilar eggshell calcification.

steps.x: **A. Asbestosis.** Asbestos job + lower zone fibrosis + plaques.

practice.stem: A 70 year old former lagger has 2 months of right-sided chest pain, weight loss and increasing breathlessness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. CT shows a large right pleural effusion with nodular pleural thickening.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the right base?
o: Stony dull percussion with reduced breath sounds
practice.e: A large pleural effusion from mesothelioma gives stony dull percussion with reduced breath sounds. Bronchial breathing suggests consolidation.

steps.x: An examination finding: what does a large effusion sound like?
Mesothelioma with a large effusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stony dull** percussion and reduced breath sounds.

elim: Bronchial breathing is consolidation (or just above an effusion).
Hyper-resonance is a pneumothorax.
A large effusion makes the note dull, not normal.
Wheeze suggests airway disease.

steps.x: **D. Stony dull percussion.** Effusion in mesothelioma.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has a chest X-ray before a hernia operation. She is well with no breathlessness. Her late husband was a builder and she washed his overalls for 20 years. The X-ray shows calcified holly-leaf shaped plaques on both hemidiaphragms and the lower lateral chest walls, with clear lung fields. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Asymptomatic calcified plaques on the diaphragm and lower lateral chest wall with clear lungs after (domestic) asbestos exposure are benign pleural plaques.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an incidental CXR finding.

clues: She is well with no breathlessness
steps.x: Domestic asbestos exposure, no symptoms, no fibrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pleural plaques**.

elim: Asbestosis needs lung fibrosis; the lungs are clear.
Mesothelioma gives pain, weight loss and an effusion.
Old TB pleurisy is usually unilateral and apical scarring is common.
Sarcoidosis gives hilar lymphadenopathy.

steps.x: **D. Pleural plaques.** Benign: reassure, no follow-up.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man who worked as a demolition labourer has asbestosis. He has 2 years of progressive breathlessness. There are fine crackles at both bases. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on spirometry?
o: Reduced FEV1 and FVC with FEV1/FVC ratio 0.55
Reduced FEV1 and FVC with FEV1/FVC ratio 0.85
practice.e: Asbestosis is a fibrotic, restrictive disease: both volumes fall with a preserved or raised ratio. A ratio of 0.55 would be obstructive.

steps.x: Spirometry pattern: obstructive or restrictive?
Interstitial fibrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Restrictive**: low FEV1 and FVC, ratio above 0.7.

elim: Symptomatic fibrosis reduces volumes.
A ratio of 0.55 is obstructive (COPD).
Low FEV1 with normal FVC means obstruction.
Reversibility suggests asthma.

steps.x: **C. Ratio 0.85 with low volumes.** Restrictive pattern.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has asbestosis after 20 years as an insulation fitter. He still smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. He asks which serious condition he is now most at risk of.
practice.q: Which condition is he at greatest increased risk of developing?
practice.e: Asbestos exposure and smoking act synergistically, multiplying lung cancer risk. Smoking cessation is the key intervention.

steps.x: A complication question.
Asbestos plus heavy smoking.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lung cancer**: the two risks multiply.

elim: Bronchiectasis is not a recognised asbestos complication.
Pneumothorax is not a typical complication of asbestosis.
PE is not specifically linked to asbestos.
TB risk is raised in silicosis, not asbestosis.

steps.x: **B. Lung cancer.** Asbestos x smoking = synergistic risk.

practice.stem: A 78 year old retired plumber has 4 years of progressive exertional breathlessness. He lagged pipes with asbestos in the 1960s and 1970s. His fingers are clubbed and there are fine crackles at both bases. His oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral lower zone reticular shadowing with pleural plaques along the diaphragms.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Lower zone fibrosis with a restrictive pattern in a man who lagged pipes with asbestos is asbestosis. Coal and silica pneumoconioses are upper zone.

steps.x: Diagnosis from history, CXR and lung function.
Asbestos exposure and lower zone fibrosis; labs show restriction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Asbestosis**.

elim: Bronchiectasis gives daily purulent sputum and coarse crackles.
Coal pneumoconiosis is upper zone in coal miners.
Sarcoidosis gives hilar lymphadenopathy, usually in younger people.
Silicosis is upper zone in stone workers and miners.

steps.x: **A. Asbestosis.** Lower zones = asbestos.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man who worked in building demolition has 18 months of worsening breathlessness. There are fine crackles at both bases. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air and pulse rate 82 bpm. His chest X-ray shows subtle basal reticular shadowing.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
practice.e: CT imaging, combined with a thorough occupational history, is the gold standard for asbestos-related lung disease and is more sensitive than CXR.

steps.x: 'Confirm': the gold standard.
Suspected asbestosis; the CXR is equivocal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT chest** with the occupational history.

elim: Bronchoscopy does not assess interstitial fibrosis well.
There is no effusion to aspirate.
Serum ACE is for sarcoidosis.
Spirometry has been done and shows restriction, not the cause.

steps.x: **B. HRCT chest.** CT + occupational history confirm.

practice.stem: A 76 year old former shipyard worker has a large left pleural effusion, chest wall pain and weight loss. CT shows nodular left pleural thickening. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Mesothelioma is confirmed by thoracoscopy and histology from a pleural biopsy. Pleural fluid cytology is often negative.

steps.x: 'Confirm' a suspected pleural malignancy.

clues: chest wall pain and weight loss
steps.x: Suspected mesothelioma; the labs show an exudate with negative cytology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thoracoscopy with pleural biopsy** for histology.

elim: Bronchoscopy looks inside the airways, not the pleura.
PET-CT helps staging but does not give a tissue diagnosis.
Cytology is often non-diagnostic in mesothelioma.
Sputum cytology does not sample the pleura.

steps.x: **E. Thoracoscopic pleural biopsy.** Tissue confirms mesothelioma.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has newly diagnosed asbestosis. He worked as a carpenter cutting asbestos boards for 15 years and still smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Smoking cessation is the most important first step because smoking and asbestos synergistically multiply lung cancer risk. His saturations do not justify oxygen.

steps.x: Initial management of asbestosis.
A current smoker who is not hypoxic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Smoking cessation** with support.

elim: He is not hypoxic enough for oxygen.
Transplant is not a first step.
Steroids do not help asbestosis.
Pirfenidone is for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

steps.x: **E. Smoking cessation.** And avoid further exposure.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has an incidental finding of bilateral calcified pleural plaques on a chest X-ray. He worked as an electrician in old buildings in the 1980s. He has no symptoms and his lung fields are clear. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. He is anxious about cancer.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Pleural plaques are benign, do not become malignant and do not raise cancer risk, so reassurance with no follow-up is correct.

steps.x: Management of an incidental finding.
Isolated, asymptomatic plaques.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reassurance, no follow-up**.

elim: Plaques need no surveillance.
Plaques are not inflammatory.
Thoracoscopy is for suspected mesothelioma.
Plaques need no imaging follow-up.

steps.x: **C. Reassurance.** Plaques are benign markers of exposure.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man has confirmed pleural mesothelioma. He is increasingly breathless at rest. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows a large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift to the left.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to relieve his breathlessness?
practice.e: A large symptomatic effusion in mesothelioma should be drained; recurrent effusions may need an indwelling catheter or pleurodesis.

steps.x: Symptom relief in mesothelioma.
A big malignant effusion is the cause of his breathlessness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Drain the effusion**.

elim: Furosemide does not clear a malignant exudate.
Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, not fluid.
Steroids do not drain fluid.
Radiotherapy does not relieve a large effusion quickly.

steps.x: **A. Drain the effusion.** Then plan for recurrence.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man who spent 25 years fitting asbestos insulation has bilateral lower zone lung fibrosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows asbestos bodies inside alveolar macrophages.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lung fibrosis?
practice.e: Asbestos fibres deposit in distal airways; macrophages release inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen species, driving chronic inflammation and fibrosis.

steps.x: A mechanism of fibrosis.
Macrophages loaded with fibres.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Macrophage-driven** inflammation: mediators and ROS cause fibrosis.

elim: Granulomas are sarcoidosis or TB.
Type III hypersensitivity is hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Elastase destruction is emphysema (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
IgE-mediated reactions are asthma and allergy.

steps.x: **C. Macrophage-driven chronic inflammation.** ROS and mediators drive fibrosis.
